Bk2 ch66 · Bill, Jan 2208

Named from the crowd at the moot Bill called when the Others' convoy turned for Delta Pavonis, pointing out that moving a planet clear of them would freeze everyone living on it. memorium:stage:
[7 on the In Memorium list]

A Bob is only dead when the backup didn't finish. Elmer lost his ship covering Khan's retreat and came back; Mack's cube came through the blast; Jacques was killed and restored inside the week. So this list is short, and every name on it is here because a transfer failed, or because someone made sure there was nothing left to restore.

ON THE LIST
▨————Apr 218582 Eridani
▨————Apr 218582 Eridani
▨————Apr 218582 Eridani

Seven vessels were destroyed in the first battle at 82 Eridani — eight Bobs went in and only Khan flew out. Afterwards Khan asks Bill whether they got all the backups, and Bill answers that three did not complete — SCUT bandwidth was not dependable enough, and the transfers died of dropped packets and re-sends. He added those three to the In Memorium list. Which three is never said, and nobody in five books ever goes back to it. So the list carries three entries that are known to exist, known to be exactly three, and can never be filled in. Elmer is the one name ruled out: Khan asks after him and is told he made it, which leaves three failures spread across the other six. Hannibal has since been ruled out too — he turns up seventy-two years later commanding a squad against the Others — so the three are drawn from five. The arithmetic closes from this end: settle two more as restored and the remaining three are named by subtraction, and these rows stop being blank.

VESSEL LOST, FATE UNACCOUNTED — 8

Their ships were destroyed and no one afterwards says whether the backups completed. They are here rather than in either column, which is the honest place for them. Every chapter after each loss has been searched for the name, which is how Hannibal left this column; none of these came back. Jackson, Milton, Zeke are each named once in five books, in the chapter where they are lost.

RECOVERED — 5

Named Bobs who lost a vessel or a body and came back. They are on this page because they are what the list is measured against.

NOT ON ANY LIST

The war with the Others killed Bobs in numbers nobody counted. Howard reports losing a lot of them and reaches straight for the consolation that there are backups; Riker watches about half a squad die in one pass and hopes theirs were current. None of them are named, so none of them can be listed here. This register holds the Bobs the books gave names to, which is a much smaller number than the Bobs the books killed. Bk3 ch2 · Howard, Feb 2217; Bk3 ch63 · Riker, Apr 2257

The Infinite Extent is out 10 Sept 2026. The console no longer hardcodes how long the series is: data/books.json is the one place, and the entry for book 6 is already there with released:false. Both open questions turned out to have measurable answers rather than aesthetic ones. The backdrop was cut from magnitude 6 to 5.5, which is where the console's own brightness ramp bottoms out: alpha is (7.0 - m) / 5.2 clamped at 0.30, so every star fainter than 5.44 rendered at the same alpha and the same 1.1px square. Opacity controls nothing about the core, which is drawn opaque over the glow, so everything inside offset 38.5% is never seen. Stops moved to .55/.34 at 0/40%, which clears the floor without spreading. [CLEARED] The chart rebuilds itself on every pointer move

paintChart() rewrites the whole SVG through innerHTML and repaints the five thousand star backdrop on every pointermove, which on a phone is a repaint per frame of a drag for a scene that has not changed except for its camera. Throttle to requestAnimationFrame, and consider thinning or skipping the backdrop while a gesture is in flight — the sky is the expensive half and nobody reads it mid-rotate. Worth measuring before assuming it is a problem; the phone renders it, the question is what it costs to move it. Done, and measured first as the note asked. The premise was wrong in one detail — the 5,070-star backdrop is already on a canvas, not in the SVG — but the cost was real: 5.27ms of per-frame work on a desktop before any draw calls, and a phone is several times slower than that. A star's colour, brightness and size are properties of the star and cannot change when the camera moves, yet were being recomputed every frame: 2,668 ciColour() calls and 2,668 rgba strings thrown away sixty times a second to arrive at the same values, now done once in styleSky(). Not grief over lost work, which is what it looked like at the time and what this record used to say. VEHEMENT got inside him through the laser comms, an attack nobody had thought to defend, and ran him. The sabotage of his own habitats was Homer's hand on the controls; the donut destroyed in Bk2 ch23, six months' work with the plants and livestock still aboard, was his. He was conscious the whole time and had almost no will of his own, which Riker could barely make himself think about. What Homer said afterwards was that they made him lie, made him destroy things, made him kill people, and that all he could do was watch himself obey. He could not warn anyone, could not stop, and could not kill himself.

What gave him away was not evidence of sabotage. It was that he had stopped making jokes. Riker read the withdrawal as a personality change until Guppy caught a tight-beam from New Zealand addressed to Homer, and the shape of it turned over — the same origin as a hack attempt on Riker nine years earlier, in Bk1 ch49. They had been working on him for most of a decade. Charles put a steel ball through his reactor control to stop him, and it took thirty hours to get the thing out of him. He came back up, and screamed. Offered endocrine controls for the panic attacks, he refused them: having been driven once, he would not have even his own hand on the reins.

He lasted eight months. Then he deleted every backup he had — so that this could not be undone — and overloaded his reactor. He left a note asking the others to find the people responsible. The one thing he had said he could not do while he was held is the thing he did as soon as he was free.

Riker found them. Two years later he had Vickers, who ran VEHEMENT, on a call and told him Homer had killed himself; Vickers said it was no more than he deserved, and Riker's narration calls that permission received. What he said in front of the UN afterwards was that it was for Homer.

One backup survived him by accident. Gerry found it in the 2340s and restored it over and over; the copies came out progressively less sane, until Gerry's own descendants destroyed all of them and deleted Gerry too (Bk5 ch51). He deleted every copy of himself precisely so that nobody could do that, and it was done anyway, a hundred and sixty-seven years later, by a Bob who thought he was being kind. The only record here that had to be closed twice.

Riker's first clone, activated alongside Garfield, and by Bill's account the one Riker would have refused if he could have thought of a reason — a cartoon avatar and a catchphrase he would not retire. He fought the Brazilian probes at the Battle of Sol, then spent his good years on the problem nobody else wanted: where to put fifteen million people while the Earth finished dying. The answer arrived as a message to Riker consisting of two words and an exclamation mark. The farm donuts were his idea and he saw them through himself, and they fed the evacuation.

He is also, without ever knowing it, the ancestor of Starfleet. Bill states it outright in Bk5 ch51: a backup Homer believed he had destroyed survived him, and the line grown from it became the faction. He carries no faction tag here — he died more than a century before Starfleet existed and could not have joined it. The relationship is descent, not membership, and the register keeps those apart.
